title: Serotonin 5-HT2B receptor agonism and valvular heart disease: implications for the development of psilocybin and related agents
abstract: During the past decade, there has been rejuvenated interest in psychedelics in combination with supportive psychotherapy as potential treatments for multiple mental disorders (e.g. mood, anxiety, and substance-use disorders) [1–3]. For example, results from mid-phase clinical studies provide preliminary evidence suggesting that psilocybin rapidly and significantly alleviates depressive symptoms in persons with Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) as well as Treatment Resistant Depression (TRD) [4,5]. The extent of improvement in depressive symptoms is noted to be clinically meaningful and sustained, representing a promising treatment approach for individuals with difficult-to-treat depression. Additional lines of research also suggest that 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) in combination with psychotherapy results in large effect-size reductions in symptoms of Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD). The magnitude of the effect reported with MDMA is greater than what has previously been reported with the two currently FDA-approved treatments (i.e. sertraline, paroxetine) [5,6]. The foregoing observations are not only breakthroughs from the point of view of symptomatic improvement, but also provide tremendous hope for persons living with severe and debilitating mental disorders. The unmet needs in the treatment of mental disorders include, inter alia, the need for treatments with a more rapid onset of clinically meaningful effect, greater effect-size improvements in psychopathology, efficacy in treatmentresistant populations, sustained benefit of therapeutic effect, greater improvement in patient reported outcomes (e.g. health-related quality of life (HRQoL), workplace and interpersonal function), improvement in positive mental health as well as treatments that are better tolerated, accessible, affordable, and cost-effective. The hope for psychedelics is their potential to address many of the foregoing unmet needs. As with all investigational treatments, however, a careful and rigorous assessment of not only therapeutic efficacy is warranted but also safety and tolerability. With respect to the safety and tolerability of psychedelics, there have been several reviews of this topic that have been recently published [7,8]. The designation of psilocybin and other classic psychedelics as controlled substances in the U.S. A. resulted in a less than adequate evaluation of the shortand long-term safety of psychedelics [9]. Recently, the FDA issued a First Draft Guidance on Clinical Trials with Psychedelic Drugs to commercial drug developers as well as academic researchers which covers a host of considerations including the need for comprehensive safety evaluation associated with psychedelic treatment [10]. The FDA has also drawn attention specifically to the need for a thorough evaluation of potential valvular heart disease (VHD) with psychedelic drug exposure. The impetus for this evaluation derives from the observation that increased 5-HT2B receptor agonistic activity in the cardiac valvular apparatus, as a result of increased serotonergic exposure and/or exposure to pharmacologic agents with functional activity at the valvular 5-HT2B receptors, have been associated with VHD. There are currently seven serotonin receptor families, all of which (except 5-HT3) are G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) [11]. The 5-HT2 serotonin receptors are further categorized into three major receptor subtypes (A, B, and C). 5-HT2B receptors are located on multiple cell types including cardiac valves which affects the structure, integrity, and function of the cardiac valves and surrounding apparatus [11]. Reports of an association between increased serotonergic availability and VHD first appeared in persons presenting with serotonin-producing carcinoid tumors [12]. In the 1960s, the first reports of drug-induced VHD appeared with ergot agents (e.g. ergotamine) which are indicated for migraine [13]. Currently, several classes of FDA-approved agents that are 5-HT2B agonists include safety information related to the potential for drug-induced VHD. These agents are indicated for Parkinson’s Disease (e.g. pergolide), hyperprolactinemia (e.g. cabergoline), and migraine (e.g. ergotamine). In addition, fenfluramine, which was combined with phentermine, as an anorectic agent (i.e. Fen-Phen) was discontinued due to drug-induced pulmonary hypertension and VHD [13–15].
